passage:
"Payal, it's midnight. What are all these boxes?"
"Old textbooks, Ma. Forty-three so far."
Vandana stepped over one. "Placements start next month. You should be practising interviews."
"I am. Ten to twelve every morning." Payal wrote First Year Physics on a box. "This is for after."
"After what?"
"After I graduate. Juniors who can't buy books will borrow these free. The college gave me a shelf in the library."
"With your name on it?"
"No name. Just a register." Payal shrugged. "When I'm gone, it'll still be there. Some girl from a village might pass physics because of a book I carried up three floors. I like that."
Vandana was quiet. Then she picked up the marker. "Your handwriting is terrible. Give me that."

qa.q: How many old textbooks had Payal collected so far?
qa.a: Forty-three so far.

qa.q: Why doesn't Payal want her name on the shelf?
qa.a: She isn't doing it for credit; she wants the library to outlast her and help juniors, and that thought pleases her.

qa.q: How does Payal balance the book project with her ambition?
qa.a: She practises interviews from ten to twelve every morning and works on the boxes at night, so the project sits alongside her placement goals.

qa.q: What does Vandana picking up the marker suggest about how she now sees the project?
qa.a: She seems to accept and even support it, moving from worry about placements to quietly helping 😊

grounding: A young woman builds a free textbook library for juniors, not for credit but to leave something that lasts, alongside preparing for placements.

passage: When I started going to the government school on Saturdays last year, I told people it was for my CV. That wasn't true, but it was easier to say. I, Siddharth, spend the other six days chasing a good rank for my master's, and I want that badly. My mother jokes that her son collects projects like stamps. But on Saturdays I sat with eight kids and a box of scrap motors, and we built a fan that barely turned. Pradeep, the quietest one, fixed the wiring before I did. This March I graduate and move away. So I spent December writing a simple guide in Hindi and English, with drawings, and trained Pradeep and another boy to run the club. Nobody there will remember my name in five years. I hope they're still building fans.

qa.q: What did Siddharth and the kids build first?
qa.a: A fan that barely turned, from a box of scrap motors.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth tell people the Saturdays were for the CV?
qa.a: He probably felt a bit shy admitting he simply cared; "for my CV" was easier to say than wanting something to outlast him.

qa.q: What choice in December helps the club outlast Siddharth?
qa.a: Writing a simple guide in two languages and training Pradeep and another boy to run the club after he leaves.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel being trusted to run the club?
qa.a: He may feel proud and more confident, since his skill at fixing the wiring was clearly noticed.

grounding: A young man mentors schoolchildren and makes sure the club outlasts him, while still chasing his own ambitions.

Volunteer coordinator's note, Green Lane Tree Trust. Sarika.
Lavanya (19) has come every second Sunday since June, even in her exam month. Today she stayed back after planting to paint small wooden labels for the sixty saplings, with the tree name and the date and no volunteer names. When I suggested she add hers to the board, she laughed and said, "The trees will be here after I'm gone. That's enough." She also mentioned she's applying for a research internship in Bengaluru and asked if I would write a reference. I said yes gladly. Next: I'll pair her with two new school volunteers so she can show them the watering schedule, and I'll send the reference by Friday.

qa.q: What did Lavanya paint on the labels?
qa.a: The tree name and the date, with no volunteer names.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's laugh and "That's enough" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She seems content, even happy, that her effort will outlast her; the trees lasting matters more to her than her name on the board.

qa.q: How does Lavanya show that giving back can sit alongside ambition?
qa.a: She keeps coming every second Sunday while also applying for a research internship and asking for a reference.

qa.q: Why might Sarika pair Lavanya with new school volunteers?
qa.a: Sarika sees Lavanya's commitment and wants it passed on, so the care continues even when volunteers change.

grounding: A young volunteer plants and labels trees without seeking credit, wanting her effort to outlast her, while also pursuing an internship.

passage:
Thursday, 11:30 pm
Finally tested the tank alarm at the primary school in Kunal's village. When the water runs low, a buzzer goes off and a red light blinks in the headmistress's room. Before this, the kids found out the tank was empty when the taps coughed at lunch.
Kunal soldered, I wrote the code on my old laptop, total cost less than a pair of shoes. No marks, no certificate, not going on my CV. Mummy asked why I spend Sundays on it with exams coming.
Honest answer: I want something I made to still be working after I'm gone. In five years some kid will wash their hands and never know my name, and I like that.
Also: entrance mock tomorrow at seven, and I still want that top institute seat badly. Both things are true.
Bhavna

qa.q: What happens when the school tank's water runs low?
qa.a: A buzzer goes off and a red light blinks in the headmistress's room.

qa.q: Why does Bhavna like that some kid will never know Bhavna's name?
qa.a: Bhavna feels content being unknown, wanting the tank alarm to outlast its maker rather than to earn credit.

qa.q: How does Bhavna hold the tank project and ambition together?
qa.a: Bhavna works on the alarm on Sundays but still sits the entrance mock and wants the seat badly, keeping both.

qa.q: How might the headmistress see the red light blinking in the office?
qa.a: The headmistress might see it as a small, lasting help that spares the children dry taps at lunch.

grounding: A young adult builds a tank alarm for a village school not for credit but so the effort outlasts them, alongside ongoing ambition.

passage: Rain was coming through the roof of the municipal school in Dharavi, and Nikita, twenty, was trying to save forty donated books from a bucket-shaped puddle. She and Aditi had spent three months collecting them for a tiny reading corner, alongside Nikita's evening prep for her management entrance exam. The inauguration was supposed to be today; the headmistress was stuck in traffic and the electricity had gone. Aditi wiped her glasses. "We could cancel. Nobody would know." Nikita shook her head. She stacked the books on two desks away from the leak and taped the handmade sign above them: READ ANYTHING. A girl in a torn uniform picked up a picture book and sat right there on the floor. Nikita watched her, heart full. She'd be gone to some B-school next year. The corner would still be here.

qa.q: How many donated books were Nikita and Aditi trying to save?
qa.a: They were trying to save forty donated books.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she watched the girl read?
qa.a: Nikita felt deeply moved and fulfilled, knowing the corner would outlast her time there.

qa.q: Why was going ahead despite the rain and power cut a good choice?
qa.a: It kept the project focused on the children, not on a ceremony, so the corner started working at once.

qa.q: How might Aditi see Nikita's decision not to cancel?
qa.a: Aditi may have been tired and ready to give up, but likely admired Nikita's commitment when the girl started reading.

grounding: A young adult builds a reading corner at a school not for credit but so her effort outlasts her, alongside her own ambitions, despite rain and a power cut.

passage: Bhupen spent every Saturday morning at the municipal school in Guwahati, teaching coding to eight class-seven students on four ancient computers. He was twenty-one, finishing his engineering degree, applying to jobs in Bengaluru. None of this would appear on his CV; he'd checked, and the college didn't give credit for it. Baljeet, the quietest in the group, had spent three weeks building a game where a rhino dodged poachers. Today it finally worked. Baljeet didn't say anything; just turned the screen toward Bhupen and grinned. Bhupen felt something settle in his chest. He had written a notes file for the next volunteer, whoever that would be: what each kid liked, what confused them, where the passwords were. He wanted the class to keep going after he left for his job. That mattered more to him than he'd expected.

qa.q: How many students does Bhupen teach on Saturdays?
qa.a: He teaches eight class-seven students.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when Baljeet turned the screen toward him?
qa.a: Bhupen felt quietly moved and satisfied, something settling in his chest at seeing Baljeet's success.

qa.q: What does writing notes for the next volunteer show about Bhupen's aims?
qa.a: It shows he wants his effort to outlast him, so the class continues after he leaves, even though it earns him nothing.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when the rhino game finally worked?
qa.a: Baljeet likely felt proud and excited, sharing it wordlessly with a grin after three weeks of trying.

grounding: A young adult mentors school kids in coding not for credit but so that his effort outlasts him, while also pursuing his career.

passage:
"You're still doing the bus-timing thing?" Nazia peered at Deepak's laptop in the college library.
"Almost done. Look, you type your stop, it tells you the next college bus."
"Is it for a project? Marks?"
"No marks. Nobody asked for it."
"Then why are you awake at 2 a.m. on it?"
Deepak rubbed his eyes. "My first year, I missed the last bus twice and walked home in the dark. I just want the juniors not to."
"Okay, but your internship interviews are next week."
"I know. I'm prepping for those too. This is different." He paused. "When I graduate, somebody will still be using it. I like that."
Nazia smiled. "You're putting your name in the About page, at least?"
"Maybe. Small font." He grinned. "Help me test it?"
"Fine. Stop number?"

qa.a: He missed the last bus twice.

qa.q: Why is Deepak awake at 2 a.m. on the bus app?
qa.a: Deepak cares that juniors don't have to walk home in the dark as he did, and he feels satisfied knowing it will still be used after he graduates.

qa.q: What does Deepak's approach do well about balancing ambition and giving?

passage:
I'm Vidya, twenty, and I want to be a surgeon. I'm ambitious; I won't pretend I'm not. But last year I started something that has nothing to do with my CV.
Every Sunday I teach basic first aid to kids in the slum near our college in Nagpur. My friend Parveen helps. We made a simple booklet with drawings, how to stop bleeding, what to do for a burn.
Nobody gives us marks. I don't even post about it. But when a ten-year-old showed me how she'd bandaged her little brother's cut properly, I felt something bigger than any exam result.
Someday I'll be gone. I'd like those kids to still know how to help someone. That matters to me as much as the surgery.

qa.q: What do Vidya and Parveen teach every Sunday?
qa.a: They teach basic first aid to kids in the slum near the college.

qa.q: What did Vidya feel when the ten-year-old showed her bandaging?
qa.a: Vidya felt something bigger than any exam result, a deep pride and meaning in helping.

qa.q: How is Vidya balancing ambition with wanting to leave something?
qa.a: Vidya keeps working toward surgery while giving Sundays to first-aid teaching that doesn't count for marks.

qa.q: How might the children's families be affected by the booklet?
qa.a: They may feel safer, since their children now know how to help with cuts and burns.

grounding: An ambitious young adult teaches first aid to children not for credit but so the effort outlasts them, alongside ambition.

University mentor's note, engineering department

Nazia, 21, is in the top five of her class and has already secured an internship. She is also, I've learned, running a small free coding club for Class 8 girls at a government school nearby, which she started with her classmate Eshaan.
She didn't mention it in her application for the scholarship. When I asked why, she said, "It's not for credit. I just want something I built to keep going after I leave."
She has written a handbook so younger students can run the club after her. She is ambitious and plans a master's abroad. The club sits alongside that, not instead.
I've asked if we can feature it in the department newsletter. She agreed, but only if Eshaan is credited too.

passage:
Diary, Sunday

Planted the last ten saplings on the college hill today. That makes one hundred since we started last year. Pema and I are both exhausted and muddy.
Someone asked if we'd get credit for this. We won't. It's not a club, not on any certificate.
I, Ganga, want to get into the civil services. I'm ambitious. I study six hours a day. But I also want to leave something that'll be here when I'm not. These trees will be big in twenty years. Some student will sit under one and not know who planted it. I like that.
Pema says I'm sentimental. Maybe. But I felt more peaceful today than after any test.

qa.q: How many saplings have Ganga and Pema planted since last year?
qa.a: One hundred.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel after planting the last saplings?
qa.a: Ganga felt more peaceful than after any test, and happy imagining future students under the trees.

qa.q: How is Ganga balancing ambition and leaving something behind?
qa.a: Ganga studies six hours a day for the civil services while also planting trees that will outlast the planting.

qa.q: How does Pema see Ganga's feelings about the trees?
qa.a: Pema teases Ganga for being sentimental, but has worked alongside every step.

grounding: An ambitious young adult plants trees not for credit but to leave something that outlasts them, alongside their ambition.

passage: In the summer before her master's applications, Arohi came home to Pandharpur with a plan she told almost nobody: a seed library in the old panchayat storeroom. She spent May going farm to farm, collecting handfuls of old millet and bean varieties the elders still grew, labelling each jar with the farmer's name. Manoj Kaka laughed at her. 'You're going abroad to study, and you're counting beans?' 'Both,' she said, writing his name on a jar of red jowar. 'These seeds will be here when I'm not.' At night she worked on her statement of purpose; by day she trained two village girls to keep the register. On the last day of May, Manoj Kaka came by with a sack of pigeon peas. 'My father grew these. Put his name on the jar,' he said.

qa.q: Where did Arohi set up the seed library?
qa.a: In the old panchayat storeroom.

qa.q: What does Arohi feel about the seed library?
qa.a: Arohi feels quietly determined and caring, wanting to leave something that lasts after she goes.

qa.q: Why was training two village girls to keep the register wise?
qa.a: It makes sure the library can outlast Arohi's time there, which is the whole point of it.

qa.q: What does Manoj Kaka's sack of pigeon peas suggest about how he now sees the project?
qa.a: He has gone from laughing to valuing it, wanting his father's name remembered in it.

grounding: A young graduate builds a village seed library meant to outlast her, alongside her study plans.

passage: Every Saturday morning Yuki took the train across Osaka to a community centre where she ran a free robotics club for middle schoolers. Her university friends were puzzled. It wasn't on her CV; she had refused to put it there. She was also competing for a tough internship at a car company, and she studied for that on the train. This Saturday, Layla, whose robot had never once moved, finally made it roll across the floor and bump into a chair. Layla screamed; the other kids cheered. Yuki found herself blinking fast. On the train home she thought: someday Layla might teach someone else, and they would never know Yuki's name. That felt right. She opened her internship notes and kept working.

qa.q: Where did Yuki run the robotics club?
qa.a: At a community centre across Osaka.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when Layla's robot moved?
qa.a: Yuki felt moved and proud, blinking fast as the kids cheered.

qa.q: What does Yuki's refusal to list the club on her CV show?
qa.a: It shows she does it to pass something on, not for credit, while still working hard for the internship.

qa.q: What might the moment mean for Layla?
qa.a: Layla, whose robot had never moved, probably feels thrilled and capable, maybe enough to keep building.

grounding: A student abroad runs a free club for younger children, wanting her effort to outlast her, while pursuing her own ambitions.

passage: The monsoon had flooded the hostel basement again, and Vishal's placement books were stacked on his bed to keep them dry. Still, at 2 pm on Saturday he pulled on his raincoat. "Coding club?" asked Abhinav from the top bunk. "They don't even give you a certificate." "I know." At the municipal school down the road, nine children in damp uniforms waited around two old laptops. Last month they had made a program that printed their names in stars. Today Vishal showed them how to save it on a pen drive and teach the next batch. "So when you're gone, we can still do it?" asked Salma, eleven. "That's the idea." He walked back through the puddles, already planning Monday's mock interview, and felt oddly steady.

qa.q: How many children waited around the laptops?
qa.a: Nine children.

qa.q: Why did Vishal keep going to the coding club without a certificate?
qa.a: He felt a quiet satisfaction in building something that would outlast him, like the children being able to teach the next batch.

qa.q: How can Vishal balance the club with his placement goals?
qa.a: He can keep the club to a fixed Saturday slot and train the children to run it themselves, so both his ambition and the project have room.

qa.q: What does Salma's question suggest about how the children see the club?
qa.a: Salma seems worried the club might end when Vishal leaves, and is relieved to hear it is meant to carry on.

grounding: A young adult runs a coding club for school children so that it will outlast him, alongside his placement ambitions.
